body.statement: Using \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{resp}}\), establish or refute the following class-uniform endpoint response result. For \((D_p,f),(D_p,g)\in\mathfrak E_s\) on the same support, with \(e=g-f\), \(\varepsilon=\lVert e\rVert_\infty\le1/2\), and normalized potentials \(\varphi_f,\varphi_g\), determine whether \[\lVert D^2\varphi_g-D^2\varphi_f\rVert_\infty\le C\varepsilon\{1+\log(C/\varepsilon)\}\] holds uniformly through \(\partial\Omega\) and whether, locally in \(C^r(D_p)\), \[\lVert\varphi_g-\varphi_f-\mathscr L_f e\rVert_{C^2(\Omega)}\le C\lVert e\rVert_{C^r(D_p)}^2.\]
body.justification: This is the genuine analytic bottleneck: Hessian inference requires an order-zero boundary-uniform response estimate and a controlled nonlinear remainder.
body.gap: CajaLopezDelgadinoKitagawa2026Stability, Theorems 1.3 and 1.5, provide potential stability and the conormal response equation; DongLeeKim2018ConormalDini provides qualitative global Dini regularity, but neither tracks the stated logarithmic Hessian modulus and quadratic remainder.
body.consumer: Resolving the endpoint theorem supplies the deterministic input for honest curvature and rank-margin bands on bounded Euclidean supports.

obligation.what_is_open: A boundary-uniform conormal Schauder--Dini estimate for the normalized linear response, with constants uniform over \(\mathfrak E_s\), and a uniform twice-differentiable neighborhood for the nonlinear second-boundary-value map.
obligation.obstruction: The frozen response handle names a boundary parametrix and dyadic cancellation but states no estimate that controls \(\lVert D^2v\rVert_\infty\) by the Dini norm of the forcing. The exact quantitative boundary cancellation and the compatible nonlinear oblique inverse are the crux, so they cannot be treated as properties of the definition.
obligation.attempted: Differentiated the Monge--Ampere equation and boundary condition, verified zero-mass compatibility, reduced the endpoint modulus to one global conormal Dini inequality, and differentiated a second time to isolate the quadratic interior and boundary data.
obligation.partial_result:
Let \(f_t=f+te\), \(F_t=\nabla\varphi_t\), \(H_t=D^2\varphi_t\), and \(\psi_t=\partial_t\varphi_t\), wherever the normalized density-to-potential map is differentiable.  Differentiating
\[
 \log\det H_t(u)+\log f_t(F_t(u))=\log\lvert\Omega\rvert^{-1}
\]
gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(H_t^{-1}D^2\psi_t)
 +\nabla\log f_t(F_t)\cdot\nabla\psi_t
 =-\frac{e(F_t)}{f_t(F_t)}.
\]
The cofactor-divergence identity and the transport equation turn this into the normalized conormal problem
\[
 -\operatorname{div}(H_t^{-1}\nabla\psi_t)
 =\frac{e(F_t)}{f_t(F_t)},\qquad
 n\cdot H_t^{-1}\nabla\psi_t=0,qquad
 \int_\Omega\psi_t=0.
\]
Its compatibility condition is exact because change of variables gives
\[
 \int_\Omega\frac{e(F_t(u))}{f_t(F_t(u))}\,du
 =\lvert\Omega\rvert\int_{D_p}e(y)\,dy=0.
\]
The desired logarithmic endpoint modulus follows if one proves, uniformly over the coefficient and boundary class, the global estimate
\[
 \lVert D^2v\rVert_\infty
 \le C\left\{\lVert r_0\rVert_\infty+
 \int_0^1\frac{\omega_{r_0}(\rho)}{\rho}\,d\rho\right\}
\]
for the preceding normalized conormal operator.  Indeed, here
\(\lVert r_0\rVert_\infty\le C\varepsilon\) and
\(\omega_{r_0}(\rho)\le\min\{C\varepsilon,C\rho^\beta\}\) for some fixed \(\beta>0\), so splitting at \(\rho=\varepsilon^{1/\beta}\) gives
\[
 \lVert D^2\psi_t\rVert_\infty
 \le C\varepsilon\{1+\log(C/\varepsilon)\}.
\]
Integrating in \(t\) produces the first requested bound.  A second differentiation gives a linear oblique problem whose interior and boundary data are quadratic in \(\psi_t\); a uniform normalized \(C^2\) inverse would then yield
\[
 \lVert\varphi_{f+e}-\varphi_f-\mathscr L_fe\rVert_{C^2(\Omega)}
 \le C\lVert e\rVert_{C^r(D_p)}^2.
\]
Thus the exact unclosed step is the stated boundary-uniform conormal Dini estimate together with a uniform twice-differentiable neighborhood for the nonlinear second-boundary-value map; neither property is contained in the frozen definition of \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{resp}}\).
